title: Saying no without saying "no"
title_target: បដិសេធដោយសុភាព — ba-de-sét daoy so-phiep
goal: Decline, apologize, and ask for help in a way that makes no one lose face — including temple etiquette and how to turn down alcohol.
bekal: decline with a reason, not with the word "no"
use សូម and …ផង to soften requests
behave properly at a wat and around monks
handle offers that keep coming back

dialogs.title: កិច្ចសន្ទនា — A neighbor's wedding invitation
dialogs.intro: Ani is invited to a wedding. She has to turn down two things and accept one — all without ever saying a bare "no". Notice that every refusal comes with a reason and is followed by an alternative.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Declining: reason first, refusal last
body: In Cambodia, as in much of Asia, a direct refusal makes people lose face. The right order is: **thank you → reason → soft refusal → alternative**. A bare "no" is almost never said to someone older or to a host.

head: Step
Khmer
Say it
rows: អរគុណច្រើន
ខ្ញុំមានការ / ខ្ញុំមិនស្រួលខ្លួន
*khnyom mien kaa / khnyom min sruèl khluèn*
ប្រហែលមិនបានទេ
លើកក្រោយបានទេ?

after: ⚠️ Notice **ប្រហែល** ("maybe") before the refusal. Adding it turns "I can't" into "I don't think I can" — and that difference is huge. It's just like English "I'm afraid I might not make it".
**The sentence ខ្ញុំមានការ** (*khnyom mien kaa*, "I have something on") is a universal excuse that nobody ever questions. You don't need to explain what it is.

⚠️ **A refusal only counts as serious the third time.** A Cambodian host will offer food again and again; your first refusal will be taken as mere politeness. If you really don't want any, repeat it with a smile: ឆ្អែតហើយ ចាស អរគុណច្រើន.

grammars.title: សូម and …ផង — two request softeners
body: Khmer softens requests from both sides: សូម in front and ផង at the end. Using both at once makes a very gentle request.

head: Sentence
Say it
Politeness level
rows: ជួយខ្ញុំផង
សូមជួយខ្ញុំ
សូមជួយខ្ញុំផង
"please help me, would you" — very gentle
ជួយខ្ញុំបានទេ?
"can you help me?" — a request shaped as a question

after: ⚠️ The question form **… បានទេ?** you know from Unit 12 is the safest way to ask a stranger for anything. It never sounds bossy, because literally it asks whether something is possible rather than giving an order.

grammars.title: Apologizing just the right amount
body: Khmer has several levels of apology, and using one that's too heavy for a small slip sounds over the top.

head: Khmer
Say it
Used for
rows: excuse me; a light "sorry"; interrupting someone
"excuse me" when passing in front of someone
ខ្ញុំសោកស្តាយ
I'm sorry — for a real mistake
that's OK (in reply to an apology)

after: សូមទោស literally means "I ask for punishment" — ទោស comes from Sanskrit *doṣa*, "fault, sin". So when you apologize in Khmer, you are literally admitting your fault and asking for the penalty. ⚠️ That's no accident: the word came to Khmer with Indian religion and law, like many words in this book.

sections.title: Etiquette at the wat and around monks

blocks.text: The wat is the center of Cambodian life, and sooner or later you'll be taken there. The rules aren't complicated, but breaking them is very noticeable — and Cambodians are too polite to tell you.

head: Rule
Details
rows: Applies to men and women alike. No sleeveless tops or shorts.
Take off shoes and hats before going in
ដោះស្បែកជើង — *dah sbaek-cheung*
Sit with your legs folded back, away from the Buddha images. The feet are considered the lowest part of the body.
Don't be higher than a monk
If a monk is sitting, you sit. Standing next to a seated monk is considered rude.
This includes not handing things straight into a monk's hands — place them on a cloth or a table.
ថតរូបបានទេ? — *that ruup baan té?*

blocks.text: Phrases to use at the wat

Khmer

ខ្ញុំមិនមែនជាពុទ្ធសាសនិកទេ

blocks.title: ⚠️ If you're Muslim in Cambodia
items: **Cambodia has a large, long-established Cham Muslim community**, and there are mosques in almost every province. The word for mosque is **វិហារឥស្លាម** (*wi-hiè 'es-laam*) or **សូរ៉ៅ** (*sou-raw*, from Malay "surau").
**Saying ខ្ញុំជាមូស្លីម** ("I'm Muslim") is almost always enough to explain why you turn down alcohol and pork. Cambodians know the Cham and won't make an issue of it.

**Being taken to a wat is still a polite visit to accept**, just like visiting a historic temple. You don't need to join in the prayers; standing respectfully is considered enough, and no one will pressure you.
